last-stone-weight.pattern: Max-heap simulation (always take the two largest)

approaches.name: Sort before every smash
approaches.idea: Simulate directly: sort the stones, smash the two heaviest, put the remainder back, and repeat.
steps: While at least two stones remain: sort them.
Remove the two heaviest `y >= x`; if `y > x`, add a stone of weight `y − x`.
Return the last stone's weight, or 0.
approaches.why: Up to n − 1 rounds, each sorting up to n stones.

approaches.name: Max-heap
approaches.idea: A max-heap gives the heaviest stone in O(log n) without re-sorting everything each round.
steps: Put all stones in a max-heap.
While the heap has at least two stones: pop `y`, pop `x`; if `y > x`, push `y − x`.
Return the remaining stone, or 0.
approaches.why: At most n − 1 rounds, each with O(log n) heap operations.

kth-largest-element-in-a-stream.pattern: Min-heap of size k (its top is the k-th largest)

approaches.name: Keep every value in a sorted list
approaches.idea: Keep all values sorted. Insert each new value at its place, and read the k-th largest from the end.
steps: In the constructor, sort `nums` into a list.
`add(val)`: binary search the insert position and insert `val` there.
Return the element at index `size − k`.
approaches.why: Finding the position is O(log n), but inserting into the middle of an array shifts up to n elements. Every value is stored.

approaches.name: Min-heap holding the k largest values
approaches.idea: Only the k largest values matter. Keep them in a min-heap: its smallest element is exactly the k-th largest. A new value either beats that smallest one (replace it) or is irrelevant.
steps: Push every initial value, popping whenever the heap grows past `k`.
`add(val)`: push `val`; if the size exceeds `k`, pop the smallest.
Return the heap's top.
approaches.why: The heap never holds more than k + 1 values. Building it costs O(n log k) once.

kth-largest-element-in-an-array.pattern: Selection: min-heap of size k, or quickselect (partition around a pivot)

approaches.name: Sort and index
approaches.idea: Sort the array; the k-th largest is at index `n − k`.
steps: Sort `nums` ascending.
Return `nums[n − k]`.
approaches.why: A full sort when only one position is needed.

approaches.name: Min-heap of the k largest
approaches.idea: Scan the array keeping the k largest values seen so far in a min-heap; at the end its top is the k-th largest.
steps: For each value, push it into a min-heap.
If the heap holds more than `k` values, pop the smallest.
Return the heap's top.
approaches.why: n pushes (and pops) on a heap of size at most k + 1.

approaches.name: Quickselect with a three-way partition
approaches.idea: Partition around a random pivot into values less than, equal to, and greater than it (like quicksort). Then the answer's position `n − k` falls into exactly one of the three parts; continue only in that part.
steps: The target index in sorted order is `t = n − k`. Search the range `[lo, hi] = [0, n − 1]`.
Pick a random pivot and partition the range into `< pivot`, `== pivot` and `> pivot` (Dutch national flag), giving the boundaries `lt` and `gt` of the equal block.
If `t < lt`, continue on the left part; if `t > gt`, on the right part; otherwise return the pivot.
approaches.why: Expected O(n): a random pivot discards a constant fraction on average, so the work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … (the worst case is O(n²) but very unlikely). The three-way split keeps it fast with many duplicates, which a two-way partition would not.

top-k-frequent-elements.pattern: Count with a hash map, then bucket sort by frequency (or a size-k heap)

approaches.name: Count, then sort values by count
approaches.idea: Count each value, sort the distinct values by count (highest first), and take the first k.
steps: Count occurrences in a hash map.
Sort the distinct values by count, descending.
Return the first `k`.
approaches.why: Counting is O(n); sorting up to n distinct values is O(n log n).

approaches.name: Count, then a min-heap of size k
approaches.idea: Keep the k most frequent values in a min-heap keyed by count; a value with a higher count pushes out the least frequent of them.
steps: Count occurrences.
For each distinct value, push `(count, value)`; if the heap exceeds `k`, pop the smallest count.
Return the values left in the heap.
approaches.why: Up to n distinct values pass through a heap of size k. The count map holds up to n entries.

approaches.name: Bucket sort by frequency
approaches.idea: A count is between 1 and n, so put each value into bucket `count`. Reading buckets from n down to 1 lists values from most to least frequent, with no comparison sort.
steps: Count occurrences.
Create n + 1 buckets; add each value to `bucket[count]`.
Walk the buckets from n down to 1, collecting values until you have `k`.
approaches.why: Counting, filling buckets and the final walk are all linear. The answer is unique, so stopping at exactly k values is safe.

k-closest-points-to-origin.pattern: Top-k selection by squared distance: max-heap of size k, or quickselect

approaches.name: Sort by distance
approaches.idea: Sort all points by `x² + y²` and return the first k.
steps: Sort points by squared distance (no square root needed: it keeps the order).
Return the first `k`.
approaches.why: A full sort when only the k smallest are needed.

approaches.name: Max-heap of the k closest so far
approaches.idea: Keep the k closest points in a max-heap by distance; when a new point is closer than the farthest of them, it replaces it.
steps: For each point, push it with its squared distance.
If the heap holds more than `k` points, pop the farthest.
Return the points left in the heap.
approaches.why: n operations on a heap of size at most k + 1.

approaches.name: Quickselect on distance
approaches.idea: Partition the points around a random pivot distance so the k closest end up in the first k slots (in any order), recursing only into the side that contains position k.
steps: Search the range `[lo, hi]` for the boundary at index `k`.
Pick a random pivot point, partition the range into distances `<` pivot, `==` pivot and `>` pivot.
If `k` falls inside the left part, continue there; if after the equal block, continue on the right; otherwise the first k slots are the k closest.
Return the first `k` points.
approaches.why: Expected linear time with a random pivot (worst case O(n²), very unlikely); partitioning is done in place (the returned copy of k points aside).

task-scheduler.pattern: Greedy: schedule around the most frequent task (heap simulation or a counting formula)

approaches.name: Simulate with a max-heap and a cooldown queue
approaches.idea: At each time step, run the available task with the most remaining copies (it is the hardest to fit). A task that just ran waits in a queue until its cooldown ends.
steps: Push the count of each task into a max-heap; keep a queue of `(remaining, readyTime)`.
Each step `t`: if the queue front is ready (`readyTime == t`), move it back into the heap.
If the heap is non-empty, pop the largest count, decrease it, and if copies remain, queue it with `readyTime = t + n + 1`. Otherwise the CPU idles.
Stop when both are empty; the answer is the number of steps.
approaches.why: T is the answer (tasks plus idles, at most about (n + 1)·tasks); each step does O(log 26) heap work. Only 26 task types exist.

approaches.name: Count the frames of the most frequent task
approaches.idea: Let the most frequent task appear `maxCount` times. Its runs split the timeline into `maxCount − 1` frames of length `n + 1`, plus a final frame holding every task that also appears `maxCount` times. Other tasks fill the gaps; if there are more tasks than gaps, no idling is needed and the answer is just the number of tasks.
steps: Count each task; find `maxCount` and `tied`, the number of tasks with that count.
The frame layout needs `(maxCount − 1) × (n + 1) + tied` intervals.
Return the larger of that and `tasks.length`.
approaches.why: One counting pass over T tasks plus 26 counts. The layout is a lower bound (copies of the top task must be n apart) and it is always achievable; when gaps overflow, every interval runs a task.

kth-smallest-element-in-a-sorted-matrix.pattern: K-way merge with a min-heap, or binary search on the value with a staircase count

approaches.name: Flatten and sort
approaches.idea: Copy every value into one array, sort it, and take index `k − 1`.
steps: Copy all n² values into an array.
Sort it and return the element at `k − 1`.
approaches.why: Sorting n² values costs O(n² log n²) = O(n² log n), and the copy uses O(n²) memory, which the problem asks to avoid.

approaches.name: Min-heap merge of the rows
approaches.idea: Each row is a sorted list. Put the first element of each row in a min-heap; popping the smallest and pushing the next element of its row produces values in sorted order. The k-th pop is the answer.
steps: Push `(matrix[r][0], r, 0)` for each row (only the first `min(n, k)` rows can matter).
Pop k − 1 times; after popping `(v, r, c)`, push `(matrix[r][c + 1], r, c + 1)` if it exists.
The top of the heap is the k-th smallest.
approaches.why: k heap operations on a heap of at most n entries.

approaches.name: Binary search on the value, counting with a staircase
approaches.idea: For a value `x`, count how many cells are `<= x` by walking from the bottom-left corner (O(n), thanks to sorted rows and columns). The answer is the smallest `x` with count `>= k`.
steps: Search `x` in `[matrix[0][0], matrix[n − 1][n − 1]]` (use 64-bit arithmetic for the middle).
Count cells `<= mid`: start at row n − 1, column 0; if the cell is `<= mid`, add `row + 1` and move right; otherwise move up.
If the count is `>= k`, set `hi = mid`; else `lo = mid + 1`.
Return `lo` — it is always a value in the matrix.
approaches.why: R = max − min ≤ 2·10⁹, so about 31 counting passes of O(n) each. The smallest x with count ≥ k must be present in the matrix, since the count only changes at matrix values.

merge-k-sorted-lists.pattern: K-way merge with a min-heap of list heads (or divide and conquer pairwise merges)

approaches.name: Collect all values, sort, rebuild
approaches.idea: Ignore the existing order: gather every value, sort, and build a new list.
steps: Walk every list and collect all N values.
Sort them.
Build a new linked list from the sorted values.
approaches.why: N is the total number of nodes. Sorting throws away the fact that each list is already sorted, and new nodes are created.

approaches.name: Merge the lists into the result one at a time
approaches.idea: Merge list 1 with list 2, then the result with list 3, and so on, using the two-list merge.
steps: Set `result = null`.
For each list, `result = mergeTwo(result, list)` (the iterative dummy-node merge).
Return `result`.
approaches.why: The growing result is walked again for every one of the k lists, so early nodes are touched up to k times.

approaches.name: Min-heap of the current heads
approaches.idea: The next node of the merged list is the smallest among the k current heads. A min-heap of the heads finds it in O(log k); after taking a node, push its successor.
steps: Push every non-empty head into a min-heap keyed by value.
Pop the smallest node, append it to the result, and push its `next` if any.
Repeat until the heap is empty; return `dummy.next`.
approaches.why: Each of the N nodes is pushed and popped once on a heap of at most k entries. Nodes are relinked, not copied.

approaches.name: Divide and conquer: merge in pairs
approaches.idea: Merge the lists pairwise like merge sort: k lists become k/2, then k/4, … until one remains. Each round touches every node once, and there are log k rounds.
steps: While more than one list remains: merge lists `i` and `i + step` for every `i` in steps of `2·step`.
Double `step` each round.
Return `lists[0]` (or null if there were no lists).
approaches.why: log k rounds of merging that each pass over all N nodes; done iteratively, it needs no heap and no recursion.

find-median-from-data-stream.pattern: Two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half

approaches.name: Keep a sorted list
approaches.idea: Insert each number into its sorted position; the median is read from the middle.
steps: `addNum`: binary search the position and insert there.
`findMedian`: with `n` values, return the middle one, or the mean of the two middle ones if `n` is even.
approaches.why: Inserting into an array shifts up to n elements; `findMedian` is O(1). Over 10⁵ calls this is up to about 5 × 10⁹ moves.

approaches.name: Two balanced heaps
approaches.idea: Split the numbers into a lower half (max-heap `lo`) and an upper half (min-heap `hi`), with `lo` holding the same number of values or one more. The median is then at the heap tops.
steps: `addNum`: push into `lo`, then move `lo`'s largest into `hi` (so every value in `lo` is ≤ every value in `hi`).
If `hi` now has more values than `lo`, move `hi`'s smallest back into `lo`.
`findMedian`: if `lo` is larger, return its top; otherwise return the mean of both tops.
approaches.why: Each add does a constant number of heap operations; `findMedian` is O(1). All values are stored once across the two heaps.

ipo.pattern: Two-stage greedy: sort by capital, max-heap of affordable profits

approaches.name: Each round, scan for the best affordable project
approaches.idea: Greedy choice: with the current capital, the best next project is the most profitable one you can afford (profits are never negative, so capital only grows). Find it by scanning.
steps: Repeat up to `k` times: scan every unused project with `capital[i] <= w` and pick the one with the largest profit.
If none is affordable, stop.
Mark it used and add its profit to `w`. Return `w`.
approaches.why: k rounds, each scanning n projects; a "used" flag per project.

approaches.name: Sort by capital, push affordable profits into a max-heap
approaches.idea: Sort projects by required capital. As capital grows, unlock projects in that order and push their profits into a max-heap; each round take the heap's best. A project once affordable stays affordable, so nothing is pushed twice.
steps: Sort project indices by `capital`.
Repeat up to `k` times: push the profit of every not-yet-unlocked project with `capital <= w`.
If the heap is empty, stop; otherwise pop the largest profit and add it to `w`.
Return `w`.
approaches.why: Sorting is O(n log n); each project is pushed once and each of the k rounds pops once.
